item.title: New Accuser Sues Foundations With Ties to Cesar Chavez
item.description:
A longtime volunteer with the United Farm Workers claims in a new lawsuit that Cesar Chavez, the civil rights leader, raped her one night in the 1970s at the union’s headquarters in central California.

The woman’s suit, filed last week in state court in California, accuses nonprofit groups affiliated with the Chavez family and the U.F.W. of negligence, sexual harassment and violations of state civil rights laws. It appears to be the first such suit of its kind since an investigation by The New York Times published in March found compelling evidence that Mr. Chavez had sexually abused, assaulted and harassed underage girls and adult women as he built the most influential farmworkers union in the United States.

The suit illustrates the legal and financial risks faced by groups with ties to Mr. Chavez in the aftermath of the revelations, particularly as California has in recent years extended the statute of limitations for victims of sexual assault to file civil lawsuits to include assaults that occurred decades ago.

California allows victims to sue not only perpetrators but also institutions that knew or should have known about abuse. Other women, some of whom have made their accusations against Mr. Chavez public, say they are also considering legal action.

The Cesar Chavez Foundation, one of the nonprofits that was named in the lawsuit, said in a statement that it had only recently become aware of it. “We are reviewing with our legal counsel and will respond in a way that stays true to our mission and values,” the statement said.

The other nonprofit that was sued, the U.F.W. Foundation, which is a separate organization from the farmworkers union itself, did not respond to requests for comment. A spokeswoman for the U.F.W. declined to comment.

A woman claiming that Cesar Chavez raped her in the 1970s is accusing nonprofit groups affiliated with the Chavez family and the United Farm Workers of negligence, sexual harassment and violations of state civil rights laws. The person who filed the lawsuit anonymously is referred to in the court document as Jane Doe. The suit contains descriptions of sexual assault.

In the lawsuit, which the woman filed anonymously as Jane Doe, she describes a previously unreported attack by Mr. Chavez in 1973. The woman, whose family lived and worked in Mr. Chavez’s compound for years, has spoken to The Times repeatedly over the last five years, and told her story on the condition that she not be named for fear of retaliation against her and her family. She is 86 years old.

She is the second woman to publicly accuse Mr. Chavez of raping them when they were adults. The other is Dolores Huerta, his U.F.W. co-founder and one of the most prominent Latina activists in the country. Ms. Huerta, 96, told The Times that Mr. Chavez had sexually assaulted her in a car in Delano, Calif., in the winter of 1966 and had previously pressured her into having sex with him in a hotel room in 1960.

Two other women, Ana Murguia and Debra Rojas, said he had molested and assaulted them when they were underage from around 1972 to 1977, starting at the ages of 12 and 13.

The accusations by Ms. Huerta and the others earlier this year set off a national reckoning over the legacy of Mr. Chavez, who became one of the most significant Latino figures in American history and who died in 1993 at 66. California has renamed the state holiday known as Cesar Chavez Day to Farmworkers Day, as officials around the country removed Mr. Chavez’s name from schools and streets, and covered or took down murals and statues bearing his likeness from college campuses and local parks.

As part of its response to the allegations, the U.F.W. announced that it was establishing a system for women to tell their stories of abuse and to start a process of reconciliation between the union and survivors. The union began a partnership with two organizations to offer survivors confidential counseling and a 24-hour bilingual crisis line. The crisis line has received calls, but a representative of one of the groups declined to say more for confidentiality reasons.

The U.F.W. Foundation is a nonprofit group that was originally called the National Farm Workers Health Group, which Mr. Chavez helped lead when it was first founded in the 1970s. The foundation now is an advocate for farmworkers and immigrants, and provides legal services for immigrants in California.

The Cesar Chavez Foundation was founded in 1966 by Mr. Chavez as the National Farm Workers Service Center. The organization, which later changed its name and expanded its mission beyond assisting farmworkers and their families, now operates Spanish-language radio stations, develops affordable housing and provides educational programs for schoolchildren in the Southwest. In its most recent federal tax filing, the nonprofit foundation listed assets of more than $260 million and revenue in 2024 of more than $40 million.

Earlier this year, the Chavez foundation issued a statement describing the allegations against Mr. Chavez as shocking and painful, and telling survivors that they believed them, honored their courage and were “very sorry for the harm you have carried in the shadows for so long.” The group has said it has been working with leaders in the field of sexual abuse and engaging in a “necessary conversation” about the organization’s identity.

The woman who filed the lawsuit said in interviews and in court documents that the assault happened around her birthday in early 1973 when she was living, along with dozens of others, at La Paz, the mountain compound near Bakersfield that was the headquarters of the U.F.W.

Her husband, a longtime Chavez ally, was working on union business in the nearby town of Delano. Her friends and colleagues threw her a birthday party in La Paz’s communal kitchen. At the party, Mr. Chavez began making sexual advances, she said. He kept giving her wine, she said, and asked her if she would let him in if he visited later that night. She said she told him no.

She eventually left the party and went to her home, she said. As she approached, she saw one of Mr. Chavez’s bodyguards outside on the steps. “The chief’s inside,” she recalled the guard telling her.

In her bedroom, she said Mr. Chavez forced himself on her and pulled her onto the bed. She said she felt powerless because of Mr. Chavez’s role as an authority figure for her family.

“He took my pants down, and that was it,” the woman said in an interview in 2023. “I didn’t have sense of self to push back.”

Her account was corroborated in interviews with people she had confided in years ago. A friend of the woman said that when he worked with her in 1994 or 1995, she told him that Mr. Chavez had sexually assaulted her and that she was still struggling to cope with the emotional trauma. Elements of the woman’s story also were consistent with emails she had written to a historian in the early 2000s.

The woman described a second episode a few years later at Mr. Chavez’s house in which she said she felt manipulated to have sexual contact with him again.

The episodes, she said, have haunted her for more than 50 years. Her struggle over whether and how to speak out has been a lingering issue in her life and has aggravated her health problems. She said she has battled thoughts of suicide over the years and tried to take her own life in 1979.

Her suit, filed in Superior Court in Kern County, the home of La Paz, seeks unspecified monetary damages and a jury trial.

The suit accuses the Chavez and U.F.W. foundations of failing to properly supervise Mr. Chavez as her landlord and her employer and of failing to prevent him from behaving in what the lawsuit describes as “an abusive, rogue and inappropriate manner.”

The suit claims that the defendants were aware of Mr. Chavez’s abuse of girls and women but hid evidence of his misconduct to prevent the wrongdoing from becoming public. It alleges that a pattern of exposing women to sexual abuse, concealing complaints and failing to take corrective action violated a state law that prohibits businesses from discriminating based on gender and other characteristics.

“Our client wasn’t the first and she wasn’t the last,” said V. James DeSimone, who is representing the woman pro bono along with the law firm led by the Los Angeles lawyer Mike Arias. “She does not want her legacy to be that she took down the U.F.W. She wants her legacy to be she’s one of the people who demanded accountability so that women in this generation don’t have to go through the same abuse.”

Miriam Jordan contributed reporting. Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Salvadorans to Keep Deportation Protections for Now, Trump Officials Say
item.description:
The Trump administration said Wednesday morning that it would not move to cancel temporary humanitarian protections for more than 170,000 Salvadorans, for now, preserving their ability to live legally in the United States and shielding them from deportation.

Temporary Protected Status, or T.P.S., allows foreign nationals from troubled nations to live and work legally in the United States and was set to expire for El Salvador on Wednesday. But the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that an announcement regarding the Salvadorans’ status would come “at the appropriate time” and that until then, “Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under T.P.S. retain protection.”

The department did not provide more information on the timing of the announcement. The administration has at times waited several days after the program’s expiration to publicize its decision.

The move stands in stark contrast to how the Trump administration has treated the roughly 350,000 Haitians whose protections expired in July. Hundreds have been deported in recent weeks, and federal officials have targeted Haitian communities in the United States with an aggressive electronic ankle monitoring campaign. Administration officials and Homeland Security’s social media accounts have churned out celebratory videos of Haitians being put on deportation flights.

The administration’s push to remove those Haitians comes even as the State Department warns travelers not to visit Haiti for any reason because of crime and other threats. The department’s travel advisory for El Salvador, meanwhile, suggests exercising normal precautions.

The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, has positioned himself as a willing White House ally central to the Trump administration’s efforts to accelerate deportations. In the spring of 2025, he helped detain more than 200 migrants deported from the United States to his country in a maximum-security prison. Experts have told The New York Times that Temporary Protected Status for Salvadorans earns Mr. Bukele political points at home, where remittances from U.S.-based family members are critical to the economy.

Still, many Salvadorans say they no longer feel safe staying with expired documentation as Immigration and Customs Enforcement sweeps across the country continue to entangle immigrants with and without legal residency.

In recent days, dozens of Latino evangelical leaders, T.P.S. holders and immigrant rights supporters have petitioned lawmakers in Washington calling for long-term protections. Some Salvadorans have begun packing, buying flights and preparing to self-deport.

“For families from El Salvador, it is a very difficult moment,” said José Palma, a Salvadoran T.P.S. holder and spokesman for the National TPS Alliance, an organization focused on defending the program. Many have lived in the United States for the past 25 years, he added, and many have established deep roots. They own cars, homes and mortgages. They have U.S.-born children in high school or heading off to college.

“We are seeing families struggling to stay stable,” he said, citing his own uncertain fate.

Agustín Quiles, who heads Mission Talk, an advocacy organization for Latino evangelicals that gathered this week in Washington, said the pastors in his network report that their members are afraid to go to school, work and church.

“There is a lot of pain, a lot of suffering,” Mr. Quiles said.

Mr. Bukele’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. He has not made a public push for the extension of T.P.S. during President Trump’s second term, but regional experts and rights groups have speculated that the issue came up when Mr. Bukele met behind closed doors with Mr. Trump at the White House in July.

The end of the program would be catastrophic for Mr. Bukele’s standing with the Salvadoran diaspora, regional experts said.

Noah Bullock, the head of the Salvadoran rights organization Cristosal, said it would be “bizarre” if the Trump administration ended T.P.S. after the moves the Salvadoran leader has made to support Mr. Trump’s agenda on migration and drug trafficking.

Mr. Bullock said the Trump administration has not only overlooked a documented pattern of human rights violations under Mr. Bukele but has also become “complicit” with his government’s abuses.

Mr. Bukele imposed a state of exception in 2022 meant to crack down on his country’s gangs that suspended due process and has resulted in the detention of tens of thousands of Salvadorans, the majority without trial. Mr. Bukele has also been credited for a sharp drop in the murder rate and a broader reduction of violence.

El Salvador appears to have reaped benefits from Mr. Bukele’s willingness to collaborate with Mr. Trump.

In April 2025, a month after Mr. Bukele accepted the Venezuelan migrants into his prison system, the U.S. State Department upgraded El Salvador’s travel advisory to its highest safety rating, officially designating it as safer than Western European nations like France. The upgrade was significant for a once-gang-plagued country whose leader is seeking to rebrand it and attract international tourism.

The number of ICE removal flights to El Salvador has jumped in 2026 compared with the year before, according to Human Rights First, a U.S.-based organization that tracks deportations. But that number is still below the number of deportation flights to El Salvador in 2022 under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. At that time, record numbers of migrants were crossing the U.S. border.

The Trump administration has already paused or terminated T.P.S. for 13 of the 17 countries once covered. The Supreme Court ruled in June that the administration could end the program for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians.

With less than two months before the midterm elections, aggressive immigration tactics have emerged as a thorny issue for Republicans. Images of people being rounded up at airports and from their cars have prompted pushback, even as members of Mr. Trump’s base have called for more heavy-handed tactics.

El Salvador was the first country designated under the T.P.S. program after Congress created it with bipartisan support and President George H.W. Bush signed it into law in 1990. The status provides safe haven for people from foreign nations engulfed in armed conflict, natural disasters and crises, and the government can renew it up to 18 months at a time.

Critics, including Mr. Trump, say the program was intended to provide only short-term relief. Immigrant rights and refugee aid organizations counter that the status has become one of the few paths to safety within an outdated and overburdened U.S. immigration system that Congress has failed to overhaul.

Daysi González, 31, a Democratic political operative and partner with Solidarity Strategies, a progressive consulting firm, has lived in the United States since she arrived in California from her native El Salvador for Christmas in 2000. She and her family entered the country on tourist visas but applied for T.P.S. after their home country was hit by powerful earthquakes that winter. She ended up staying for decades.

Ms. González said she would have applied for longer-term residency if she had been able to, but the program does not provide a legal pathway to lawful permanent resident status.

Now, she has been posting videos on social media chronicling what could be her final days in the United States. On Tuesday, she was searching for flights and waiting to hear back from her employer on whether she could keep her job.

“Without confirmation that I can legally work, that I can renew my license — living here will just be too dangerous,” she said.

item.title: Joseph Rice, Lowcountry Lawyer Who Took On Big Tobacco, Dies at 72
item.description:
Joseph F. Rice, a formidable negotiator who helped states extract multibillion-dollar settlements from tobacco companies and the opioid industry, fundamentally reshaping how corporate America is held accountable for wrongdoing, died on Sept. 3 in Mount Pleasant, S.C., a Lowcountry town near Charleston. He was 72.

A representative for his firm, Motley Rice, said the cause was a cardiac event, which he experienced while at his desk in his law office.

Mr. Rice wore cowboy boots and Southern charm at the bargaining table, where he squared off against hot shot corporate lawyers over astronomical sums of money.

“They were petrified of him,” Jayne Conroy, a lawyer with Simmons Hanly Conroy, an Illinois-based firm that collaborated with Motley Rice, said in an interview. “He was smarter than everyone else. But he was also charismatic and likable, so he could get people to do things and make deals.”

An old school lawyer who drove a pickup truck and rattled off ideas into a Dictaphone — sometimes while riding his horse — Mr. Rice preferred the pragmatism of the negotiating table over courtroom theatrics.

To strengthen his hand, he relied on a novel legal strategy: States and local governments, he argued, had public nuisance claims against corporations, in addition to product liability claims brought by individual consumers. The governments were victims because they were footing the bills for the damage those products caused.

With tobacco, billions of dollars in Medicaid funds were spent treating smoking-related illnesses. With opioids, enormous sums of taxpayer dollars went toward addiction treatment, emergency medical care and other consequences of the epidemic.

By bringing state and local governments into the lawsuits as plaintiffs, Mr. Rice shifted the narrative from individual injuries to the sweeping public costs of corporate misconduct.

It was an audacious tactic that posed an existential threat to entire industries.

“The idea of states going after tobacco companies because they had to divert funds to address smoking-related injuries — that was a totally wild idea,” Nora Freeman Engstrom, a Stanford Law School professor, said in an interview. “Joe was a mastermind at legal theory and the detail guy who got things done.”

The strategy Mr. Rice helped pioneer is still being used to take on powerful industries. Motley Rice represents state attorneys who are suing social media companies for allegedly harming the mental health of teenagers.

For lawyers, it is an incredibly lucrative method.

Mr. Rice’s firm stood to make as much as $2 billion for its work on the $206 billion settlement between tobacco companies and states in 1998, according to The Post and Courier of Charleston, S.C.

“Yeah, it’s a lot of money,” Mr. Rice told The New York Times. “But nobody gave us a chance in hell when we started out.”

The big payday, he argued, was deserved.

“Why should the lawyers who carried the burden and led the fight not be paid like a chief executive officer of a corporation?” he said.

Legal scholars say the enormous payments to lawyers were a side effect of deals that ultimately benefited public health.

The tobacco settlement included provisions for reducing cigarette advertising, contributing to lower smoking rates, especially among teenagers. The opioid settlements led to tighter monitoring of narcotic drug shipments, as well as funding earmarked for treatment programs.

“Is there some abuse in the plaintiff’s bar? Absolutely,” Professor Engstrom said. “But on balance, are more people alive than otherwise would have been? In my view, yes.”

Joseph Fred Rice was born on March 25, 1954, in Winnsboro, S.C., about 30 miles north of Columbia. His father, Donnie Rice Jr., was a textile worker. His mother, Betty (Dunlap) Rice, worked in real estate.

His grandfather, a mill paymaster, collected books on law.

“When he had a spare dollar, or actually probably 50 cents back then, he would go buy a law book, and he’d read up on the law,” Mr. Rice told Law360, a legal news site, in 2019. “I had some of those law books when I was growing up, so I got interested, I think at first because it was intriguing.”

During high school, he worked in textile mills, where he first learned the art of mediation.

“Sometimes the guy driving the forklift truck and the guy setting the machines up were not necessarily buddies,” he said last year in an interview with Super Lawyers, a legal information site. “If one was late, it hurt the other one, and we had some negotiation to do in a situation like that.”

He enrolled at the University of South Carolina, graduating in 1976 with a bachelor’s degree in business administration and a transcript that reflected the good times he had as president of his fraternity, Alpha Tau Omega.

Mr. Rice applied to South Carolina’s law school and was offered a spot in a summer program for borderline applicants; he was eventually admitted. (The law school was named after him in 2023.)

He graduated in 1979 and got an offer from Ron Motley, a lawyer at Blatt & Fales in Barnwell, S.C., to work on a case involving nuclear fuel rods.

While Mr. Rice was soft-spoken and folksy, Mr. Motley was a showman who once wore a lab coat to cross-examine a doctor.

Still, they formed an enduring and lucrative partnership in scores of product liability cases, beginning with hundreds of suits filed against asbestos companies in the 1980s.

The asbestos litigation became a blueprint for pursuing entire industries at once — an undertaking that required Mr. Rice to marshal vast coalitions of plaintiffs, lawyers and experts, as well as state attorneys general and municipal officials.

On the other side of the table, defense lawyers had confidence that Mr. Rice could deliver what they ultimately wanted: peace.

“I viewed him as a tough negotiator, but he knew how to close a deal,” Sheila L. Birnbaum, the national co-counsel for Purdue Pharma, the maker of OxyContin, said in an interview. “He always had that charming Southern mannerism that held him in good stead.”

Mr. Rice married Lisa Summer in 1979. She survives him, along with their daughter, Ann E. Rice Ervin, a lawyer at Motley Rice; a sister, Ann Rice Phillips; a brother, Don Rice III; and a grandson.

Mr. Rice worked until he died, but he did find time to enjoy his enormous wealth. He owned a ranch and a 100-foot yacht, and he was among the biggest fans (and financial supporters) of the University of South Carolina football team.

He also indulged in cigars.

“Everybody says, ‘Well, you sued over cigarettes and there’s tobacco in that,’” Mr. Rice said in the Super Lawyers interview. “I said, ‘I sued the cigarette industry. I didn’t sue the cigar industry.’”

item.title: Here’s How the Postal Service Could Refuse to Deliver Your Mail Ballot
item.description:
The U.S. Postal Service is poised to play a critical new role in determining which mail ballots are delivered to voters this fall. If the Supreme Court allows President Trump to move forward with an executive order he issued in March, the agency would screen ballots after they are submitted by election officials and would deliver only those that comply with new rules. Two dozen states have sued to halt the plan, calling it unconstitutional.

Here’s how the process would work, according to notices issued by the Postal Service:

1

Each ballot envelope must:

Include the official Election Mail logo

Be able to be scanned by Postal Service machines

Bear each voter’s unique Postal Service bar code

Some states already voluntarily follow some of these guidelines. But for those that do not, redesigning ballot envelopes this late in the process and getting them approved by the Postal Service could be logistically challenging or impossible and cause delays, according to election officials.

2

VOTERS

The Postal Service will deliver mail ballots only to the voters on these lists.

Each list must include three key pieces of information for each voter:

Name

Address

Unique bar code

This adds a new step before mail ballots can go out. The chief election officer in each state is responsible for uploading lists in a standardized format or delegating that task to other officials. The portal is still under construction. The Postal Service has said it is expected to be ready soon for states to begin to voluntarily comply.

3

These bulk mailings can contain tens of thousands of ballots, often in plastic-wrapped pallets. The ballot envelopes must comply with the new design requirements and must have bar codes that match the list of approved mail voters that states submitted to the portal.

If a ballot envelope is not in compliance, the mailing will be rejected and returned to election officials. Election officials must address and fix any errors before resubmitting the mailing, which would delay the delivery of ballots to voters.

item.title: Tate Brothers Must Remain in U.S. Jail Until Extradition Case Is Decided
item.description:
A federal magistrate judge in Miami ruled on Wednesday that Andrew and Tristan Tate posed a flight risk and will remain behind bars as they fight extradition to Britain to face charges of rape and sex trafficking.

The decision, while expected, was another blow for the Tates, right-wing influencers known for their embrace of misogyny and hypermasculinity. The brothers, dual citizens of Britain and the United States, became wealthy by peddling online pornography and self-help courses on fitness, money and dating.

The magistrate was not swayed by the Tates, who took the stand during a detention hearing last month. They insisted that they needed to be released from near-solitary confinement at a Miami federal detention center to assist their lawyers in contesting the allegations against them, which they have repeatedly denied.

In a 30-page order published Wednesday, Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis wrote that even if the wealth that they have flaunted online was exaggerated, “they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction.”

She also wrote that they have no ties to Miami and that most of their family is overseas in Dubai and Romania, adding to their flight risk.

In recent years, the Tates have encountered widening legal scrutiny in Romania and Britain, where prosecutors have asked the United States to extradite them on new allegations involving four victims. Federal marshals arrested the brothers on July 18 outside a bare-knuckle boxing event in downtown Miami.

The Miami court has not set a date for an extradition hearing. The British government has until Sept. 16 to provide documentation to its U.S. counterparts on the allegations against the Tates.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Tates maintained they were innocent of all the charges against them.

“They are now facing an extraordinary situation in which they are being held thousands of miles from Romania while Romanian proceedings continue, deadlines approach, an additional indictment is said to be imminent, and their own Romanian lawyer says he cannot properly prepare,” a spokesman said in a statement.

The brothers have faced legal problems since their arrest in Romania in 2022 on allegations of human trafficking, among other serious crimes.

Earlier this month, Romanian prosecutors announced a new indictment against the brothers in the investigation they began in late 2024.

They accused Andrew Tate of recruiting a 15-year-old girl in 2012, housing her in Britain and Romania, and exploiting her for financial gain through pornographic webcam material. They accused Tristan Tate of being complicit in sex trafficking and said that the brothers had made more than $1.2 million from exploiting the girl. Andrew Tate is also accused of having sex with another 15-year-old.

In 2024, British authorities charged the brothers with rape, assault and human trafficking. A Romanian court agreed to extradite them to Britain, but only after the resolution of the cases against them in Romania.

In all, the Tates face allegations involving seven victims in Britain, prosecutors have said. In a court filing, the government described in graphic detail allegations that the brothers would choke women, sometimes until they passed out, before raping them.

Their lawyers in South Florida have described the Tates’ prosecution as political, decried their detention conditions as inhumane and argued to the court that the brothers’ “extraordinary notoriety and recognizability” would make sneaking out of the United States nearly impossible.

In 2025, Romanian prosecutors granted them permission to travel abroad after they had previously argued that the brothers were a public danger and a flight risk. Support from Trump administration officials played a crucial role, according to a New York Times investigation.

During last month’s detention hearing, a lawyer for the brothers told the magistrate that England “is trying to cut in line by circumventing the Romanian orders.”

U.S. prosecutors also noted that Andrew Tate had bragged online that he had multiple passports and of his ability to evade law enforcement. And they warned that the brothers’ purported wealth — including private jets, yachts and sports cars — could support a life on the run.

Abbie Waxman, a prosecutor on the case, told the magistrate that Andrew Tate had “unfettered access to travel and funds,” including cryptocurrency. “He’s not tied to anything,” she said.

On the stand, the brothers downplayed their purported wealth and brash online personas. Andrew Tate testified that his online statements were “hyperbolic exaggeration for comedic effect,” the hallmark of an alter ego he assumes to generate money.

Defense lawyers also said a Mexican passport held by Tristan Tate in the name of Vladimir Scorpius was a Halloween prop and a reference to a fictional James Bond villain. The government said that the passport had a document number that could have been obtained only by requesting it from the Mexican government, something Tristan Tate denied doing.

The magistrate noted that even if their social media personas were just posturing, “there is nonetheless a dearth of competent, credible evidence” that the brothers would not be a flight risk.

item.title: What’s Missing From Trump’s Midterm Convention
item.description:
One thing is missing from President Trump’s midterm gathering for Republicans this week: any semblance of official party business that forms the backbone of traditional quadrennial conventions.

Essentially, Mr. Trump has stripped out all the perfunctory, yet necessary, parts of a typical presidential convention and kept the made-for-TV elements.

Only once before in modern political history, in 1982, has a national party held a midterm-year gathering in advance of the midterm elections. That event, held by Democrats, went so poorly that the next party chairman called such events “places for mischief” and canceled plans to do it again in 1986.

In Dallas, there will not be a roll call of states awarding delegates to a presidential nominee. There won’t even be a presidential nominee. Or voting delegates. Forget about subcommittees to determine the party’s rules and credentials.

Republicans will not be debating their party platform, though they did not really do that at the last two presidential conventions, either. By now, the party’s platform is generally whatever Mr. Trump decides it is.

Instead, the two-day gathering in Dallas is set to be a pair of six-hour — though perhaps much longer — advertisements for Mr. Trump and his political acolytes. The speakers are a parade of Trump supporters, many of whom are either in his cabinet or on the ballot this November.

Party conventions in presidential years usually take place in the summer, are scheduled to avoid the Olympic Games and are meant to be held when there are few other compelling TV options. This event comes after Labor Day and will compete for national attention against the first two nights of the N.F.L. season.

The 1982 Democratic midterm conference, as it was called then, followed similar events in 1974 and 1978 that were held in December, after the midterm elections. They were essentially kickoff events for the coming presidential elections — though in 1978, Senator Edward M. Kennedy upstaged President Jimmy Carter with a speech that foreshadowed their contentious primary campaign.

Last year Ken Martin, the Democratic National Committee chairman, floated holding a midterm convention, but the idea was quietly dropped.

Some things in Dallas will look familiar. Vice President JD Vance, who is set to speak on Thursday night, will play the role of potential future presidential contender. His speech will be inspected for both his loyalty to Mr. Trump and indications of his possible ambitions for 2028.

And you can bet that Mr. Trump will preside over a balloon drop, or maybe two of them. They were known to be among his favorite parts of the 2016 and 2024 conventions — and a spectacle that had to be skipped in 2020 when Republicans moved their convention outdoors because of the coronavirus pandemic.

item.title: William Anderson, Doctor and Civil Rights Leader in Georgia, Dies at 98
item.description:
William G. Anderson, a doctor who in 1961 set aside his medical practice in Albany, Ga., to lead a movement against the city’s entrenched system of racial segregation, attracting national attention and the involvement of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., died on Aug. 16 at his home in Detroit. He was 98.

His daughter Valé Henson confirmed the death.

The Albany Movement, a coalition of the city’s Black and civil rights groups, appeared at a pivotal moment in the struggle against Jim Crow segregation, coming between early successes like the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-56 and later triumphs like the Birmingham campaign and the March on Washington, both in 1963.

With Dr. Anderson, an osteopath, as its leader, the movement in Albany pushed for integration of local businesses and tested federal laws against discrimination in interstate bus travel. Over the course of a year, the police arrested some 1,200 demonstrators who belonged to the movement, including Dr. Anderson, who was briefly jailed.

As the arrests mounted and national news media swarmed into town, Dr. Anderson decided to call an old friend, Dr. King, for assistance. “I realized that I got all these people into jail; now how am I going to get them out?” he told the McClatchy news service in 2009. “I realized, I’m in over my head.”

Dr. King and his lieutenant Ralph Abernathy spent months organizing in Albany and were arrested alongside Dr. Anderson.

Although Dr. Anderson had been born in the nearby city of Americus, he had received his medical training in the north and had only recently returned to Georgia to practice. He chose Albany because it had few Black doctors.

He had not been active in the civil rights movement until that point, but he felt compelled to address the blatant racial injustices that hindered his ability to provide medical treatment. As a Black man, he could not practice at the hospital, the only one in town — even though white doctors often refused to see Black patients or did so only reluctantly.

He did most of his work through house calls, visiting homes that often lacked running water and electricity. On one occasion, he delivered a baby at night, under the illumination from the headlights of his car parked outside.

In early 1961, a group of young activists from the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee came to Albany to organize a movement. Though they faced resistance from the Black establishment, they found ready recruits among Albany’s restive youth, who began testing segregation through actions like sit-ins and were arrested in the process.

“I came out of my office and, after watching these kids be intimidated, I went and started marching,” Dr. Anderson said in a 2019 interview with The DO, a publication about osteopathy. “They weren’t marching for themselves; they were doing it for myself, my family, my patients and my community.”

That fall, several Black organizations, including the N.A.A.C.P., met to discuss an alliance, which they called the Albany Movement. They elected Dr. Anderson as its president; the gathered leaders felt that, as a doctor serving exclusively Black patients, he was somewhat insulated from white reprisals.

Dr. Anderson proved an effective spokesman for the Albany Movement. He undertook an extensive speaking tour of the West Coast, and in 1962 he went on the NBC Sunday talk show “Meet the Press” to explain the movement’s goals to millions of viewers.

When one panelist, James J. Kilpatrick, an ardent segregationist who was editor of The Richmond News Leader, asked him whether Black protesters had “invited” their arrests, Dr. Anderson pushed back.

“Yes,” he said, “if expressing your constitutional rights is inviting arrest, then yes.”

When Dr. King and Mr. Abernathy left Albany in the summer of 1962, Dr. King said that the movement had failed in the face of a wily local white police chief, Laurie Pritchett, who refused to be baited into using violence against protesters.

Dr. Anderson and other organizers saw things differently. Over the next few years, away from the glare of national attention, Albany’s white establishment quietly dismantled many of the city’s most flagrant segregation laws and allowed Black candidates to run for local office.

William Gilchrist Anderson was born in Americus on Dec. 12, 1927, to John Anderson, who worked in insurance, and Emma (Gilchrist) Anderson, who was an administrator with the school system in Sumter County, where Americus is located.

He was 15 when he entered Fort Valley State College (now Fort Valley State University), a historically Black institution in Fort Valley, Ga., but in 1944 he left to enlist in the Navy, where he served as a medical corpsman during World War II.

After his discharge, he married Norma Lee Dixon, who also became a civil rights activist, in 1946, and attended the Atlanta College of Mortuary Science. During that time, he befriended Dr. King, who was studying at nearby Morehouse College and had been a childhood neighbor of his wife.

In 1949, Dr. Anderson received a bachelor’s degree in biology from the Alabama State College for Negroes (now Alabama State University). Seven years later, he received a doctorate in osteopathy from Des Moines University in Iowa, and, after a year’s residency in Flint, Mich., he settled in Albany.

His wife died in 2007. In addition to Ms. Henson, Dr. Anderson is survived by four other children, A. Laurita Faison, William Anderson II, Frank Anderson and Darnita Anderson Hill; 10 grandchildren; and seven great-grandchildren. Three of his children and three of his grandchildren have degrees in osteopathic medicine.

After the Albany Movement ended in 1962, Dr. Anderson and his family moved to Detroit, where he became the city’s first Black surgical resident and later opened a surgical practice. He taught at the Michigan State University College of Osteopathic Medicine and, in 1994, became the first Black president of the American Osteopathic Association.

As a result of his conviction for obstruction of justice during the Albany protests, Dr. Anderson was a felon — a mark of distinction, he said, for his service to the movement.

“My involvement with Martin Luther King Jr. and Ralph David Abernathy earned me this dubious distinction,” he wrote in his 2025 memoir, “The Making of a (PARDONED) Felon During the Civil Rights Movement in America: The Physician Who Helped Heal American Democracy.”

“It is a badge I have worn proudly, as have many others who participated in the civil rights movements of the 1950s and 1960s,” he wrote.

item.title: 60 Posts in 10 Hours: How Trump’s Social Media Reflects His Version of Reality
item.description:
Just before noon on a holiday weekend, while many Americans were at the beach, President Trump’s social media account roared to life. In what has increasingly become his weekend habit, he unleashed a daylong barrage of posts that put the bully in the modern bully pulpit.

There were images of Mr. Trump intimidating Canada’s prime minister with a hockey stick, personally bombing enemy targets and patrolling dark streets with killer robots. There were maps showing the United States taking over other countries, and maps renaming a state. There were attacks on the “Dumocratic Party” and tributes to himself as “the Greatest President of All Time!”

The 60 messages posted online over 10 hours and 41 minutes offered a window into Mr. Trump’s own unique reality, one anchored not in fact but in an expression of ego. For years, his social media feed was said to be a mirror of his id. But with A.I., it has become the manifestation of how he wants to be seen in a more visual, visceral way than ever before — as a warrior, as a conqueror, as a historical figure, as a younger and thinner and more muscular version of himself.

In Mr. Trump’s digitally enhanced version of the world, he is a giant in every way, a man who defeats every adversary, overcomes every obstacle and sinks every putt. He not only redraws the map of the world but vanquishes the heavens themselves. “The Moon Is Ours,” declared one post last weekend with an image of the earth’s only satellite. Another posted a few weeks ago showed him leading an extraterrestrial alien in shackles.

The rat-a-tat of ever wilder, ever more outrageous posts each weekend has become a fixture of the president’s second term, seen more and more as a barometer of his mental state. Mr. Trump’s critics, who never considered him a model of stability in the first place, now point to these frenetic bursts of fantasy and vanity as proof that the 80-year-old president is deteriorating further with age.

It is a measure of how much Mr. Trump has changed the nature of the presidency that any of this has become routine. Past presidents believed they had a duty to carry themselves with a certain dignity befitting the office. Mr. Trump sees politics like the cage match he sponsored this summer at the White House.

Indeed, the images he posted over the Labor Day weekend included one with his face on Hulk Hogan’s rippling body. Another posted a day later imagined a grinning Mr. Trump easily winning an arm wrestling match against Mr. Hogan, the flamboyant wrestling star who died last year.

“He floods the zone with so much of it that we’ve become numb to just how bizarre it is,” said Sarah Matthews, Mr. Trump’s former deputy White House press secretary. “An 80-year-old president is spending a ridiculous amount of time consuming and reposting endless A.I. fan fiction portraying him as the biggest, strongest and most important person alive. It feels like we’re genuinely watching his brain rot in real time.”

To his defenders, Mr. Trump is a master of baiting his adversaries, getting them to react. “It’s called: We do a little trolling,” as Mr. Trump once put it. The more out there the message is, the more his supporters cheer. As abnormal as the images that he posts may be for a president, Mr. Trump’s allies argue that they convey a certain raw, earthy quality that suits an age of no-holds-barred politics.

“With all due respect, the media and President Trump’s other critics have spent more than a decade complaining about his use of social media,” said Alex Bruesewitz, a former campaign aide. “They keep calling it ‘unpresidential,’ but if the president is doing it, it is presidential by definition. I think most Americans appreciate the authentic and transparent way he uses these platforms.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​”

Violence is a recurring theme in Mr. Trump’s feed. He relishes the idea of himself as a tough man staring down anyone who gets in his way. He smashes Iran with a giant hammer. He pilots a spacecraft blasting the planet. Most arresting was his post last weekend showing him in a hockey uniform with a stick towering over a fallen Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and taunting, “Get up, Governor,” as if Canada really were the 51st state that he says he wants to make it. That one, unsurprisingly, further inflamed international tensions.

As Mr. Trump surely knew it would. It is hard to imagine any other president picturing himself physically assaulting the leader of an ally. But for Mr. Trump, who has been unable to force Mr. Carney to back down in a tariff fight, the cartoonish image allows him to present himself as winning even when he is not.

Never mind that he may cry foul if anyone else were to picture him as the target of violence. Goaded by Mr. Trump, the Justice Department indicted James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, for a social media post showing seashells spelling out the numbers “86 47,” interpreting the image as a threat to the president.

“This is truly unhinged behavior from the President of the United States,” Representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine Democrat, wrote online after the Carney post. “And I don’t want to hear ‘oh, it’s just Trump being Trump’ or that he’s ‘trolling.’ Enough. None of this is normal or okay. Republicans cannot keep shrugging this off. Congress, the Cabinet, and everyone around him has a responsibility to stop enabling this dangerous behavior and start asking whether he is fit to hold this office.”

The White House shrugged off the criticism. “Truth Social is the most powerful and popular social media platform in the world because it serves as President Trump’s authentic voice, where he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context,” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said in a statement, using the name of the president’s social media platform.

In fact, by traditional measures, Truth Social is nowhere near as popular as major social media platforms like Facebook or X and its traffic has slumped since last year. But it has effectively become the town hall for Mr. Trump’s MAGA followers and therefore plays an outsize role in American politics. Either posting himself or approving posts crafted by aides, Mr. Trump uses it as his main outlet for presidential messages to the world.

Last Sunday was a striking day on Truth Social but increasingly typical of the president’s weekend blitzes, when he has fewer staff members around him and more unscheduled time. While at his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., Mr. Trump started posting at 11:54 a.m. and kept returning to his account in staccato bursts throughout the day. At 1:47 p.m., he posted six messages within two minutes. From 2:40 p.m. to 3:43 p.m., he circulated another 27 posts. He continued through the evening, only letting up after his final one of the night at 10:35 p.m.

They were the kinds of posts that are common on the internet, just not normally from a head of state — impertinent, insulting, scornful, belligerent and sometimes out-and-out wacky. They offered a Rorschach test for followers, funny to those who admire what they see as Mr. Trump’s wry sense of humor, delusional to those who think he has lost his mind.

As with Canada, his many posts on Iran that day portrayed his war as he would like it to be, not how it really is. In the actual Middle East outside of his control, Mr. Trump is stuck in a quagmire with no clear end in sight. In the virtual Middle East of his own creation, Mr. Trump is a triumphal commander in chief bludgeoning Iran into submission.

The flurry of posts last weekend included an image of a bomber attacking with the caption “Bye bye, Kharg,” referring to the Iranian island, and a map showing the Strait of Hormuz labeled “New U.S. Territory.” Another featured supposed before-and-after maps of Iran with the latter showing the country in the shape of Mr. Trump’s own wavy-haired profile.

Maps, in fact, were big with Mr. Trump as he played with his phone that day. He posted a map of the north half of the Western Hemisphere showing the U.S. flag superimposed on Canada, Mexico, Greenland, Iceland, Cuba and all of Central America and the Caribbean islands, all under the label “United States of America.”

Canada, Mexico and Greenland have gotten used to this sort of provocation, but Iceland was shocked to be included, and summoned the U.S. ambassador to complain. “There is nothing funny or normal about making fun of the sovereignty of states,” Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir of Iceland told reporters.

Even as he showcased his imperialist ambitions abroad, Mr. Trump asserted his authoritarian instincts at home, posting multiple maps and images of him peremptorily renaming the state of New Mexico as “New America,” something he has no power to do. As with the Icelanders, the New Mexicans were not amused. “Oh hell no!” Representative Melanie Stansbury, a Democrat, wrote online.

While Mr. Trump’s posts regularly influence domestic politics and foreign policy, he also uses A.I. to promote grandiose visions of himself as a superhero, a pope and at one point last spring a Jesus-like figure. Last weekend’s posts included one that he has circulated before offering his own chart ranking American presidents, with him, naturally, at the top as “The Greatest.” Another post asserted: “He Will Go Down In History As the Greatest President of All Time!”

Mr. Trump, who avoided the draft during the Vietnam War with a diagnosis of bone spurs provided by a doctor who was one of his father’s tenants, particularly enjoys presenting himself as a martial hero.

In an image posted last month, Mr. Trump wore the military uniform that he never wore in real life standing between Generals George S. Patton and Douglas MacArthur. George Washington has become a regular guest in Mr. Trump’s world lately. Sunday’s burst included images of him with the father of the country on horseback and in the Oval Office.

The advent of A.I. has allowed Mr. Trump to go further than the mainly written social media posts of his first term. “Trump has always treated social media as a window into whatever he is thinking at that moment, but A.I. makes that window far more vivid and frankly more disturbing,” said Ms. Matthews, his former press aide. “And it feels like the more difficult reality gets for him, the more A.I. slop he posts.”

Mr. Bruesewitz, the former campaign aide, called Mr. Trump an innovator who is paving the way to the future of politics. “President Trump is the first true social media president,” he said. “He has always adapted to the times, using new technology and platforms to take his message straight to the public. His A.I. posts generate enormous attention whenever he hits send.”

No one would debate that they are attention generators. One way or another, that seems to be the point.

item.title: Iran’s Strikes on Base in Jordan Caused Limited Damage, U.S. Officials Say
item.description:
Iran’s bombardment overnight Tuesday of a military base in Jordan used by American forces resulted in “minimal” damage to equipment and caused no deaths, two U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

But the officials warned that some service members may come forward in the coming days to report traumatic brain injuries, a common feature of such strikes.

Eighteen American service members have been killed and scores have been injured since the war began more than six months ago. The Pentagon has provided little information about U.S. casualties unless they were serious, citing operational security.

The barrage of strikes on the base were the latest volley in what is becoming a regular series of tit-for-tat strikes between Washington and Tehran, as Iran’s leaders show a willingness to escalate the conflict.

Iran targeted Jordan after the U.S. military said on Tuesday that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attempted strikes on a U.S. Navy warship.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps called the strikes a “punitive operation” and said that they would “continue,” according to Iranian state media.

The Jordanian military said that it had intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles and that two had fallen in unpopulated areas. But the two U.S. officials acknowledged that the base in Azraq, Jordan, was hit.

The attacks occurred three days after Iran made its first known attempt at striking an American military vessel.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed responsibility for the attacks on a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer, saying it fired ballistic missiles at them for “harassing Iranian ships.”

Both countries appear to be stuck in a cycle that is draining U.S. air defenses and deepening Iran’s economic crisis.

As of last month, the Pentagon had used more than 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the war and had fewer than 1,700 interceptors left, according to two people briefed on the stockpile levels who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details. The United States produced about 600 interceptors in all of 2025.

At the same time, President Trump’s naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, an economically vital waterway, is making it nearly impossible for Iran to ship oil, its main source of revenue.

Mr. Trump has tried to pivot from a military campaign to one focused on choking its economy, but fighting has flared in recent days as each side jostles for control of the strait.

U.S. military officials have vowed to strike three Iranian ships for every two vessels hit by Tehran. But Iran has continued to fire on ships, throttling the world’s oil supply, to preserve one of its biggest sources of leverage.

The result has been a stalemate.

The U.S. military’s Central Command said the Iranian tankers it targeted on Tuesday were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the I.R.G.C. and its regional proxies,” referring to the Revolutionary Guards. It said the attacks came after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a Navy warship twice in two days.

item.title: Trump’s Convention Offers an ‘Investor Experience’ and Pricey Tickets
item.description:
President Trump’s unusual midterm convention is also an unusual fund-raising opportunity for the Republican Party.

To begin with, the two-day extravaganza in Dallas is more like a cash-for-seat reception than it is a traditional experience for delegates who carry out party business at a normal presidential-year convention.

Mr. Trump’s convention will still have unofficial delegates, even if they have no formal business to conduct — and some state parties are charging them for the right to attend, much as fund-raising events charge those who want to attend a V.I.P. reception.

One county Republican Party in Texas advertised an “honorary delegate” package for $20,000. Michigan’s Republican Party charged people $5,000 a ticket for floor passes to become an “honorary delegate.”

“This is not a traditional delegate position and does not involve convention voting or official delegate responsibilities,” the marketing materials for the Michigan G.O.P. read. “Instead, the Honorary Delegate designation is a special recognition that grants you an exclusive experience that most attendees will never have.”

Donors began checking into luxury hotels like the Ritz-Carlton and the Crescent Court in Dallas on Tuesday afternoon. Some conservative fund-raisers said they expected many of the party’s financial powerhouses not to attend. Several Republican megadonors, including the Dallas Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson and the hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin, are not scheduled to appear, according to their representatives.

Those who do trek to Texas for the Republican National Committee’s event are set to be treated to an extensive “R.N.C. investor experience,” according to a booklet of events distributed to donors and obtained by The New York Times.

Receptions and meals will be hosted by several Trump cabinet members, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy; Scott Turner, the housing secretary; and Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Vice President JD Vance will headline a “Liberty Luncheon” on Thursday for R.N.C. donors.

Other satellite events are happening around town. The Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, is set to host several briefings for its donors, including a fund-raising lunch with Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, according to a document obtained by Punchbowl News. The outlet reported that another event would feature a fireside chat with Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the House majority leader, who will be joined by Texas donors like Harlan Crow and Ross Perot Jr.

Mr. Trump is also scheduled to participate in two events, according to the White House: one on Wednesday afternoon with MAGA Inc., his high-powered super PAC, and a Thursday round-table for the Republican National Committee.

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas is throwing a fund-raiser featuring Ken Paxton, the state’s Republican nominee for Senate, at the Ritz-Carlton on Thursday afternoon, according to a copy of the invitation viewed by The Times. The event will raise money for a Cruz-aligned super PAC that is spending for Mr. Paxton.

There will be plenty of libation, too. A welcome reception on Tuesday evening was thrown by the Rockbridge Network, a donor network aligned with Mr. Vance. One event set for Wednesday evening is called “The Great American Midterm Party” and features hosts like former speaker Kevin McCarthy, the tech donor Joe Lonsdale and the president’s son Donald Trump Jr., according to an invitation seen by The Times.

A party on Thursday is scheduled to be thrown by Republicans from Houston — which is hosting the actual next convention, in the summer of 2028.

Emily Davies and Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: Hunter Biden’s Crypto Offering Plummets Upon Launching
item.description:
Hunter Biden’s new novelty crypto token flopped Wednesday morning, losing more than 95 percent of its value in a matter of hours of its launch.

The son of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. had criticized President Trump’s own such token, called a memecoin, as a “grift.” Critics immediately said the younger Mr. Biden’s was no different.

In a social media post Tuesday night on X, Mr. Biden presented his new coin partly as a mechanism to make charitable donations. He did not address whether and how he would personally benefit, but creators of memecoins can profit from transaction fees or if their own tokens rise in value.

Memecoins are akin to collectibles, with no intrinsic value. Their worth is driven purely by demand and speculation.

Mr. Biden’s coin, $LAPTOP, started trading at $37.26, jumped to $222.75 within minutes, then plummeted to $1.34 by midafternoon, according to CoinMarketCap, a website that monitors crypto prices.

The token’s name refers to his laptop, the source of controversy when it was discovered in a computer repair shop and its contents leaked before the 2020 election. Materials on the computer added fuel to concerns about his foreign business dealings; the Biden campaign rejected the accusations.

In a late-afternoon post on X, Mr. Biden blamed predatory traders and technical problems for driving up the token’s price. He said the price had stabilized to a “healthy” level.

Mr. Trump took in a whopping $636 million from sales of his $TRUMP memecoin last year, according to his latest financial disclosure. That represented more than a fourth of the minimum of $2.2 billion in revenue he reported.

But many purchasers of that coin lost out when it crashed in value, according to Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm. As of the middle of last year, 58 buyers had gained a total of about $1.1 billion in profits. Some 764,000 crypto wallets, most with small holdings, lost money, the firm’s data shows.

The president’s coin, having once peaked around $74, was selling Wednesday for $2.15, slightly more than Mr. Biden’s. Melania Trump’s token, introduced along with the president’s on the eve of Inauguration Day, was selling for 11 cents, down from a high of around $14.

Critics of memecoins claim they are often no more than “pump-and-dump” schemes, where creators and early buyers hype the coin, then cash out before the value tumbles. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission can bring civil charges if it finds fraud.

Mr. Biden denounced Mr. Trump’s coin as a scam in his media post while trying to drive up interest in his own offering, flagging an article in The Wall Street Journal about its debut.

“Why would I ever want to support a memecoin? Why something that has been so misused by grifters?” he wrote. He discouraged buying his coin as an investment, saying that “you should not expect me or anyone else to make this token more valuable for you.”

Instead, Mr. Biden, who says he is sober after a history of drug addiction, promoted it as a symbol of “resilience, redemption and recovery.”

As the coin nose-dived, social media critics let loose. “You, Trump, Melania, and the others are just ripping people off who support you,” one wrote on X. “You are truly no better.”

item.title: Military Aide Accidentally Deploys Emergency Slide on New Air Force One
item.description:
A military aide accidentally deployed an inflatable emergency slide on the new Air Force One on Wednesday, delaying President Trump’s departure to Dallas, according to a person familiar with the episode.

Mr. Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews that officials were just checking on the slide. He did not acknowledge it had been inadvertently deployed.

“They want to make sure everything works perfectly,” he said, noting that he would be delayed only about 15 minutes.

Mr. Trump eventually took off on the plane to Dallas, where he is attending the Republican midterm convention.

“As the president has said, the slide was checked out to make sure everything works perfectly,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said in a statement. “Air Force One is on its way to Dallas so he can deliver his much-anticipated speech to a raucous and sold-out crowd.”

The White House declined to share any details on the incident, but the emergency escape slide in the Boeing 747-8 operates in a fashion similar to an airbag, as it is rapidly inflated in an emergency with high-pressure compressed gas cylinders.

After the slide has been deployed, it has to be carefully folded and inspected before it can be reinstalled and the inflation mechanism has to be reset and certified.

But to get a plane back in service more quickly, a replacement emergency slide device could be installed with certified technicians, according to documentation about the system published by aviation parts suppliers.

The new Air Force One, a 747-8, has an unusual evacuation slide because one of its doors is high off the ground and requires an abnormally long slide that has to be extendable, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The deployment of the inflatable slide marked the latest challenge in Mr. Trump’s efforts to fly on the new presidential aircraft, which was donated by the Qatari government.

Once the U.S. government took ownership of the plane, it was quickly retrofitted so that the president could start flying it as soon as possible. The New York Times reported that the Qatari jet lacked defensive capabilities that the older models have.

Concerns about the new plane’s capabilities came under more scrutiny when Mr. Trump took it to the NATO summit in Turkey in July. Multiple people with knowledge of the matter said that there had been a security concern about his flying aboard the Qatari plane.

Mr. Trump declared that he would fly on one of the older presidential aircraft for his departure, instead of the Qatari jet that he had flown aboard to Turkey, for “old time’s sake.”

Although he boarded the older plane at the airport in Ankara, Turkey, it later emerged that the president had been whisked off it and onto a military jet, leaving the older Air Force One aircraft as a decoy flight.

Eric Lipton contributed reporting.

item.title: New Mexico’s Name Is Older Than the U.S. Trump Still Wants to Change It.
item.description:
Long before the first 13 states ratified the Constitution or General George Washington crossed the Delaware, and well before the Mayflower sailed toward Cape Cod, a rolling patch of high desert in what would someday become the American Southwest was known as Nuevo México.

This week, New Mexicans are practically screaming that fact and hoping their collective uproar reaches the White House, where President Trump has mused about renaming their state “New America.”

The suggestion makes no sense, residents fume, because the Land of Enchantment’s official toponym predates both the United States and Mexico, the target of Mr. Trump’s latest round of rebranding. The president has no authority to change the state’s name, but the mere proposition — which he reiterated in at least nine Truth Social posts — constituted fighting words to proud New Mexicans.

“No, just no — never,” said Rob Martinez, New Mexico’s state historian, who invoked a 17th-century rebellion against Spanish colonizers to underscore just how seriously New Mexicans are taking this. “We will start another Pueblo Revolt.”

While Mr. Trump had the power to force federal entities to recognize his rechristening of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America, he cannot do the same with a state. Any change to New Mexico’s name would require approval from both chambers of the state’s Legislature and then from New Mexico voters.

In interviews, more than a dozen New Mexicans were unanimous: It’s not going to happen.

New Mexico is not just a name, residents said. It’s a reflection of the state’s heritage and its cherished multicultural identity.

Scholars trace the “Mexico” portion of the state’s moniker to the Aztec language of Nahuatl, and Spanish priests and soldiers began referring to the area as Nuevo México in the 1500s. When New Mexico joined the union in 1912, it enshrined its anglicized name in the first article of its state Constitution.

“We were here before there was a United States of America,” said Randy Rodriguez, a 67-year-old shopkeeper with a horseshoe mustache and a store full ofcowboy hats and antique spurs.

To Mr. Rodriguez, who counts the Spanish explorer Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca as an ancestor, the floated name change feels personal. “They’re erasing history,” he said.

Mr. Trump has offered little explanation for his reasoning beyond memes, including one that showed a map that warped the boundaries of the proposed “New America” to take in large chunks of Arizona and Texas. New Mexico is a heavily Democratic state that has voted against Mr. Trump in the last three presidential elections.

“Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA,” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!”

But in Santa Fe, America’s oldest capital city, established more than 150 years before the United States, residents found the proposition neither prestigious nor beautiful.

“If you change it to New America, you’re taking away part of our culture,” said Elizabeth Tapia, a jeweler at a Native American artisans market in the historic Santa Fe Plaza on a recent evening.

The new name, said Ms. Tapia, a member of the Santo Domingo Pueblo tribe, “sounds white.”

“Why does everything have to have ‘America’ in it?” chimed in Audrey Crespin, another vendor.

Jo Christen, the owner of a Santa Fe gift shop, said she believed the idea might finally unite New Mexicans of all political stripes against “a common enemy.”

So far, it has done just that. Both major parties’ candidates for governor forcefully condemned Mr. Trump’s idea.

And at least some of Mr. Trump’s voters concur.

“I think that sucks,” Donnell Brox, who was visiting Santa Fe from Las Vegas, said of the president’s posts. “I love Trump, but I don’t always agree with him.”

Gabriel Sanchez, a political science professor at the University of New Mexico — not, he noted, the University of New America — said he saw Mr. Trump’s proposal as another attempt to distract the public from a flagging economy and the war with Iran.

Even though the proposal is far-fetched, Mr. Sanchez said, “people are talking about it. I had a 25-minute conversation with my mail carrier.”

Mr. Sanchez said the president’s focus on the word “Mexico” was racist. He suggested that names of British origin — New York and New Hampshire, perhaps — should also be on the chopping block.

The state’s poet laureate, Manuel González, said he figured Mr. Trump was trolling. Still, he resented the suggestion that New Mexico was somehow not American enough.

“We are already America,” he said. “All the people who come together to make this place special is also what makes America special.”

Mr. Martinez, the state historian, said he would simply refuse to use Mr. Trump’s new appellations.

“It’s still Lake Ontario, it’s still the Gulf of Mexico,” he said.

And, he added, it will always be New Mexico.

“I am the state historian of Nuevo México,” he said. “We are never changing our business cards.”

item.title: Election Officials Grapple With Uncertainty as Supreme Court Considers Mail Ballot Plan
item.description:
Election officials in Madison, Wis., mailed 18,000 ballots on Tuesday, more than a week ahead of the state’s targeted date, just to get them out the door. In Weber County, Utah, officials are considering setting up distribution centers for voters to retrieve their mail ballots and bypass the Postal Service completely.

Across the country, election officials are grappling with the confusing implications of the Trump administration’s proposed mail ballot screening plan, which would allow the Postal Service to determine which ballots can be delivered to voters.

A federal judge has halted implementation of the system, which has been challenged as unconstitutional by two dozen states. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and allow it to go forward ahead of the midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.

While they wait for the court’s order, local election officials are trying to sort out how they would comply with the new rules, which would require states to use federally approved envelopes with bar codes unique to each voter and upload voter data to an online Postal Service portal, which is not yet operational.

“Quite frankly, we don’t even really have a way to prepare because we don’t know when that ruling is going to come down, and then we’re going to get state guidance, and then we are crunching up closer and closer to Election Day,” said Lisa M. Deeley, the Democratic vice chair of the Philadelphia City Commissioners, which runs elections and voter registration for the city. The city is planning to start mailing ballots next week.

“It’s just chaos,” she added.

Some states, including North Carolina, Delaware and Alabama, have already mailed out their ballots, raising serious questions about how they could retroactively comply with the new system if it is put into place.

It is not clear whether or how the Postal Service would verify previously mailed ballots if the new rule goes into effect.

“We have not been provided any further information regarding their process for verifying the ballots,” said Kristin Mavromatis, the spokeswoman for the board of elections in Mecklenburg County, N.C.

On Wednesday, the chief election officials in seven G.O.P.-controlled states filed a brief to the Supreme Court, arguing that it was too close to the midterms to make any major changes to how elections are conducted.

The brief, which was signed by the Republican secretaries of state in Kentucky, North Dakota, South Dakota, Georgia, New Hampshire and Kansas, as well as the lieutenant governor of Utah, broke with the Trump administration’s effort to significantly restrict mail voting ahead of the 2026 elections. They were joined by 26 current county and local election officials and five former election officials.

In signing the brief, the secretaries of state in Kansas and South Dakota found themselves on opposite sides from those states’ attorneys general, who were part of a Republican-led state coalition arguing in support of the administration’s mail voting plans. The Missouri Association of County Clerks and Election Authorities also broke with their attorney general in signing the brief.

Their disagreement was not necessarily on the policy; rather, it was on the timing.

“Attempting to implement the rule now will almost certainly lead to mistakes, delays and confusion for both voters and election officials,” the brief states.

Many election experts say the plan could make it nearly impossible for some Americans to vote by mail because it would create impediments to the delivery of their ballots.

“It would be massively disenfranchising, and it would serve no real purpose, because the government didn’t make any showing that this rule is actually going to prevent any fraud, or even that they could put their rule in place,” said Richard L. Hasen, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specializes in election law.

Mr. Hasen said that the rule would especially hurt rural, disabled and elderly voters who often cannot easily get to polling locations.

Justin Roebuck, the Republican County clerk for Ottawa County, Mich., a conservative district with one-quarter of its voters casting mail ballots, said the rule appeared to do little to accomplish what the Trump administration has argued is its purpose — to increase voting security.

“So we are actually not accomplishing what the end goal was, but we are going to inconvenience millions of voters across the country — certainly, thousands in my community,” he said.

Under the Constitution, states are responsible for carrying out elections. The states that are challenging the Trump administration’s new plan say that it creates a federal role in elections because the Postal Service would reject ballot envelopes that do not comply with the new standards and send them back to local and state officials to fix.

“That comes dangerously close to playing a role in the administration of elections, which the Postal Service has always, always eschewed,” William Hensley, a former Postal Service official who worked with local election officials on best practices for ballot delivery, said.

The Postal Service has denied taking on a new election administration role, saying that states have complete control over voter registration data.

The agency did not respond to requests for comment this week. In a statement on Friday, the postmaster general, David Steiner, said, “Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery.”

Some of the requirements in the rule — such as those that would standardize federal ballot envelopes and create unique bar codes for voters that the Postal Service can easily read automatically — could improve the process, some elections officials and lawyers said. But, they added, it is impossible to accomplish those changes in time for the Nov. 3 elections.

“These are all good things,” said Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis County, Mo. “But if people haven’t been doing it, it can’t be implemented overnight.”

Missouri is one of 12 states that joined the Postal Service in defending the rule in federal court. The state has said it would be able to comply if the Supreme Court gives the Trump administration the green light, although Mr. Fey said he told the state’s top election official that some counties could not comply because they do not have federally approved envelopes or Postal Service bar codes.

In Utah, a deeply red state that votes almost exclusively by mail, some local officials are discussing abandoning mail voting entirely if the Supreme Court allows the Postal Service to restrict the practice.

With envelopes already printed and ballots coming soon, Ricky Hatch, the Republican clerk in Weber County, Utah, said that it is too late for his county to comply with the proposed federal requirements. Officials are considering setting up backup ballot distribution centers.

“We’re going to have to figure out how are we going to get these ballots into the hands of the voters,” Mr. Hatch said, adding: “It will be expensive and challenging and some voters will be disenfranchised, and it will be confusing.”

In their brief to the Supreme Court, the G.O.P. election officials noted that many of the states had already designed and printed their mail ballot envelopes.

Getting new envelopes would normally take four to eight weeks from vendors. A crush of thousands of municipalities needing new materials could stretch that timeline to 12 to 16 weeks, well beyond Election Day in November, the officials noted.

Some election officials have also expressed alarm about the Trump administration’s requirement that states upload their voter data to a Postal Service portal. The Postal Service would then only deliver ballots to those on the lists.

Elections are usually administered by individual counties, and standardizing voter registrations even within a single state is a challenge, local officials noted.

Some Texas counties have struggled with the state’s election management system that was launched last summer, said Dyana Limon-Mercado, the Democratic clerk in Travis County, one of the largest in the state.

Ms. Limon-Mercado said that certain voter registrations have been disappearing from the state system. At one point, the state system did not accept hyphenated names, she said. “I have no confidence that this state system that is also unstable and still buggy is going to connect to some federal system that we haven’t seen yet or tested yet,” she said.

Zach Montague and Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.
